={{sc|Syn.}} Accoutrements, equipments, paraphernalia, gear, decorations, frippery.

'''trapping-attachment''' (trap′ing-a̤-tach″ment), ''n.'' A metal or other appurtenance or mounting for horse-trappings. ''L. Jewitt'', in Art Jour., N. S., IX. 345. [Rare.]

'''trappings''', ''n. pl.'' See ''trapping''.

'''Trappist''' (trap′ist), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< F. ''Trappiste'', so called from the abbey of ''La Trappe'' in France: see def.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A member of a monastic body, a branch of the Cistercian order. {{smaller|It is named from the village of Soligny-la-Trappe, in the department of Orne, France, where the abbey of La Trappe was founded in 1140 by Rotrou, Count of Perche. The abbey soon fell into decay, and was governed for many years by titular or commendatory abbots. De Rancé (1626–1700), who had been commendatory abbot of La Trappe from his boyhood, became its actual abbot in 1664, and thoroughly reformed and reorganized the order. The rules of the order are noted for their extreme austerity, and inculcate extended fasts, severe manual labor, almost perpetual silence, abstinence from flesh, fish, etc., and rigorous asceticism in general. The order was repressed in France during the Revolutionary and Napoleonic periods. There are branch monasteries in France, Belgium, Great Britain, Italy, etc., and two in the United States (Abbey of Gethsemane, Kentucky, and Melleray, Iowa).}}

'''2.''' [''l. c.''] In ''ornith.'', a South American puff-bird or fissirostral barbet of the genus ''Monasa'' (or ''Monacha''). Also called ''nun-bird''. Both are book-names, given from the somber plumage, which also suggested ''Monasa''. See cut under ''nun-bird''.

'''Trappistine''' (trap′is-tin), ''n.'' [< F. ''Trappistine'', a nun of the order of La Trappe; as ''Trappist'' + ''-ine''<sup>2</sup>.] 1. A member of an order of nuns, affiliated with the Trappists, founded in 1827, and established chiefly in France.—2. [''l. c.''] A sweet cordial made at a monastery of Trappist monks. Compare ''Benedictine'', 2, ''chartreuse'', 2.

'''trappoid''' (trap′oid), ''a.'' [< ''trap''<sup>3</sup> (''trapp'') + ''-oid''.] Resembling trap; having more or less the character of a trappean rock.

{{smaller block|The workers of past centuries used to crush the ore in saucer-like hollows in the solid, tough, ''trappoid'' rock, with rounded granite crushers.
{{right|''Nature'', XLI. 140.}}}}

'''trappour†''', ''n.'' See ''trapper''<sup>2</sup>.

'''trappous, trappose''' (trap′us, -ōs), ''a.'' [< ''trap''<sup>3</sup> (''trapp'') + ''-ous''.] Trappean. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''Trapp's formula.''' Same as ''formula of Christison'' (which see, under ''formula'').

'''trappure†''', ''n.'' See ''trapper''<sup>2</sup>.

'''trappy''' (trap′i), ''a.'' [< ''trap''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Of the nature of a trap; treacherous. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|The fences might have increased in size, however, without being made ''trappy''.
{{right|''Daily Telegraph'', Nov. 13, 1882. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''trap-rock''' (trap′rok), ''n.'' A rock consisting of trap; trap.

{{smaller block|Round North Berwick ''trap-rocks'' rise in all directions.
{{right|''Harper's Mag.'', LXXIX. 790.}}}}

'''trap-seine''' (trap′sān), ''n.'' A trap-net specially adapted to take fish working down an eddy. [Rhode Island.]

'''trap-stair''' (trap′stãr), ''n.'' A narrow staircase, or step-ladder, surmounted by a trap-door.

'''trap-stick''' (trap′stik), ''n.'' '''1.''' A stick used in the game of trap; an object resembling such a stick.

'''trap-tree''' (trap′trē), ''n.'' The jack-tree: so called because it furnishes a glutinous gum used as bird-lime. In some parts of the East the fiber of the bark is used for fishing-lines, cordage, and nets.

readings.c3s3:
¶
'''trash'''<sup>3</sup> (trash), ''n.'' [Perhaps ult. a var. of ''trace''<sup>2</sup> (ME. ''trais'', ''trays'', etc.).] 1. A clog; anything fastened to a dog or other animal to keep it from ranging widely, straying, leaping fences, or the like.

{{smaller block|Your huntsmans lodging, wherin hee shall also keep his coomples, liams, collars, ''trashes'', boxes.
{{right|''Markham'', Countrey Contentment (1615), i. 1.}}}}

Hence—2. A clog or encumbrance, in a metaphorical sense.

'''trash'''<sup>3</sup> (trash), ''v. t.'' [< ''trash''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.''] To hold back by a leash, halter, or leaded collar, as a dog in pursuing game; hence, to retard; clog; encumber; hinder.

{{smaller block|Without the most furious haste on the part of the Kalmucks, there was not a chance for them, burdened and ''trashed'' as they were, to anticipate so agile and light cavalry as the Cossacks in seizing this important pass.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Flight of a Tartar Tribe.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To trash a trail''', to destroy the scent by taking to water: a stratagem practised both by game and by man when pursued. [Western U. S.]}}

'''trashery''' (trash′ėr-i), ''n.'' [< ''trash''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ery''.] Trash; rubbish; odds and ends.

{{smaller block|Who comes in foreign ''trashery''
Of tinkling chain and spur.
{{right|''Scott'', Bridal of Triermain, ii.}}}}

'''trash-house''' (trash′hous), ''n.'' A building on a sugar estate where the cane-stalks from which the juice has been expressed are stored for fuel. ''Simmonds.''

'''trash-ice''' (trash′īs), ''n.'' Broken ice mixed with water. ''Kane.''

[< ''trash''1 + ''-ery''.] Trash; rubbish; odds and ends. {{smaller block|Who comes in foreign ''trashery'' Of tinkling chain and spur. {{right|''Scott'', Bridal of Triermain, ii.}}}} '''trash-house''' (trash′hous), ''n.''
